proposal.policy_prompt_for_action:
When reproducing the demonstrated planar stick route, the policy generally selected the correct chronological leg and correctly recognized the preceding arrival, but placed bypass turns and gap arrivals one to several centimetres away from the demonstrated endpoints. Some bypass commands incorrectly preserved the current y coordinate; others extended a leg beyond its turn. Gap commands sometimes used an approaching sample as the arrival, and one final command followed a shaft or trail location instead of the final free tip. The retained demonstration and completed-leg count supplied the required history. These failures concern SUFFICIENCY of the action reconstruction procedure, not a missing memory transition.

Strengthen the reconstruction procedure with an explicit evidence-assignment and validation stage before selecting the next endpoint. Identify the stick as the narrow rigid extension attached beneath the hand, and locate the centre of its distal end. Do not use the lowest pixel of the hand, the centre of the shaft, the nearby white trail, or a red ground marker. Track this same physical feature through the demonstration. An occluded distal end is an unavailable tip measurement, not permission to choose another nearby feature. Use the reported initial TCP, projected into the initial execution view, to verify which visible feature represents the free tip and its height; this check does not license a constant image-space offset for other poses.

For each turn, explicitly assign evidence to the incoming and outgoing legs before fitting. Use the preceding arrival and samples strictly before the turn for the incoming segment, and samples strictly after the turn together with the following arrival for the outgoing segment. For example, a first turn bracketed by the early demonstration samples uses the start and pre-turn sample on one side, and the post-turn sample and first gap arrival on the other. Apply the same bracketing rule at later turns. A sample nearest a nominal temporal boundary is not automatically the endpoint. Fit both x and y components freely: neither an apparently vertical shaft nor an approximately axial image trajectory justifies fixing a world coordinate to its current value. Retain the existing prohibition on constant-speed temporal interpolation.

Before accepting an inferred intersection, project it and the fitted segments back into the retained views. Check that correctly identified incoming and outgoing tip observations lie on their respective fitted segments, in chronological order, and that the endpoint lies beyond the last incoming observation and before the first outgoing observation along the route. Reject intersections obtained by extending only one segment, assigning a departure sample to an arrival leg, or treating a rounded trail corner as a straight tip trajectory. Use interior, clearly visible tip samples preferentially for direction estimation; uncertain or occluded observations must not receive the same weight as clear distal-tip measurements. If the two directions remain underconstrained, use the adjoining arrival evidence and other views of the same geometric location rather than inventing a longer clearance move.

For gap endpoints, gather all demonstrated visits to that same static gap and use their arrival and departure evidence jointly to localize the common position. In particular, a clear final visit can constrain an earlier partly occluded arrival. Share the gap location, not its chronological occurrence: each visit still consumes its own leg. Do not impose this equality on bypass turns merely because they go around the same obstacle end; outward and return turns can differ. A still-approaching tip sample supplies a constraint on the incoming segment, not the full arrival position.

For the stopping point, require an explicit distal-tip identification in the final frame and corroborate it with the preceding frame. Perform the calibrated z=0.07 ray-plane calculation on that identified pixel, then reproject the result to verify the calculation and feature selection. If a purported pixel and purported world coordinate disagree under the calibration, discard the pair rather than treating either as an authoritative endpoint. Retain the existing route-order, height, orientation, arrival-tolerance and purposeful terminal-wait rules. Do not add route-specific coordinate tables, extra motion subdivisions, or extra clearance.
proposal.refused: The reports repeatedly requested individual turn coordinates and frame-specific clauses. Those numerical answers are not new historical facts: the memory already retains the complete ordered demonstration, and every reported completed-leg update was correct. Adding endpoint coordinates derived from recorded execution waypoints would make annotation depend on information unavailable to the deployed policy. No memory fields or transition rules therefore change. The generalizable evidence-assignment and localization problems are passed on as action changes instead of a separate exception for each failed cycle. Several requested safeguards—preserving repetitions, distinguishing ground-marker height from tip height, fitting both sides of unsampled turns, and prioritizing the final tip—already exist; they are retained and operationally strengthened rather than presented as missing history. Literal pixel-to-coordinate examples are not adopted: at least one reported final-tip pixel is inconsistent with its claimed world endpoint under the supplied calibration. Nor is a guarantee that sparse or occluded imagery uniquely determines every endpoint to one centimetre asserted; the reports establish localization errors, not that an additional memorized fact would resolve them.

policy_prompt_for_action.modify_from: For each usable demonstration frame, locate the lower free end of the stick, not the upper shaft, robot housing, marker or trail.
policy_prompt_for_action.modify_to: Identify the stick as the narrow rigid extension beneath the hand and track the centre of its distal end through the demonstration. At the initial act cycle, project the reported TCP into the current execution view to check which visible feature represents the free tip at z=0.07 m; do not transfer a constant image-space offset to other poses. For each usable demonstration frame, measure that same distal-tip feature, not the lowest pixel of the hand, the shaft centre, robot housing, marker or trail. An occluded distal end is an unavailable tip measurement, not permission to substitute a nearby feature.

policy_prompt_for_action.modify_from: For an unsampled turn, fit the incoming and outgoing planar path directions from tip positions on their respective legs, using multiple frames wherever available. Extend those fitted segments to their intersection to recover the shared endpoint; with noisy observations, use a joint least-squares fit with a shared endpoint.
policy_prompt_for_action.modify_to: Before fitting an unsampled turn, assign each measurement to its chronological leg. Use the preceding arrival and samples strictly before the turn for the incoming segment, and samples strictly after the turn and the following arrival for the outgoing segment. Do not treat a departure sample as evidence of the preceding arrival. Fit the incoming and outgoing planar directions using multiple frames wherever available, preferentially using clear interior distal-tip measurements; downweight uncertain measurements and exclude occluded-tip substitutions. Fit both world x and y freely: an apparently axial image trajectory or vertical shaft does not justify preserving a current world coordinate. Extend both fitted segments to their intersection to recover the shared endpoint; with noisy observations, use a joint least-squares fit with a shared endpoint.

policy_prompt_for_action.modify_from: Project the recovered endpoint back into the demonstration to check consistency with both segments and the demonstrated obstacle side.
policy_prompt_for_action.modify_to: Project the recovered endpoint and both fitted segments back into the demonstration. Check that the assigned distal-tip observations lie on their respective segments in chronological order, that the endpoint follows the last incoming observation and precedes the first outgoing observation along the route, and that the demonstrated obstacle side is preserved. Reject an endpoint supported by extending only one fitted direction, misassigned arrival/departure evidence, or a rounded trail corner treated as a straight tip trajectory. If directions remain underconstrained, use adjoining arrival evidence and other demonstrated views of the same geometric location; do not invent a longer clearance move.

policy_prompt_for_action.modify_from: The retained starting view or a clearly observed visit to the same gap can supply an additional localization constraint without merging separate route occurrences.
policy_prompt_for_action.modify_to: Gather arrival and departure evidence from all demonstrated visits to the same static gap to constrain its common location, including the retained starting view and any clear final visit. A still-approaching sample constrains the incoming segment, not the arrival position. Share the gap location without merging chronological occurrences: each visit consumes its own leg. Do not impose shared coordinates on bypass turns merely because they pass the same obstacle end.

policy_prompt_for_action.modify_from: For the final endpoint, prioritize the actual lower tip in the final demonstration frame, corroborated by preceding arrival frames, and project it onto z=0.07 m. Do not extrapolate beyond it to a nominal gap coordinate or nominal leg length.
policy_prompt_for_action.modify_to: For the final endpoint, explicitly identify the distal-tip centre in the final demonstration frame and corroborate the feature identification with preceding arrival frames. Apply the calibrated z=0.07 m ray-plane calculation to that pixel and reproject the resulting coordinate to check numerical consistency; reprojection alone does not establish that the chosen feature is the tip. fields.name: demonstration
fields.description: At the video cycle, record the ordered list of all supplied demonstration frame labels, including the initial and final frames. Preserve this list unchanged throughout execution. These images specify the entire demonstrated route, including obstacle sides, intermediate turns, reversals, repeated visits and the stopping point; do not replace it with an unordered set of visited places. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V99"]
fields.annotation: At the video cycle, record the ordered list of all supplied demonstration frame labels, including the initial and final frames. Preserve this list unchanged throughout execution. These images specify the entire demonstrated route, including obstacle sides, intermediate turns, reversals, repeated visits and the stopping point; do not replace it with an unordered set of visited places. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V99"]

fields.name: completed_legs
fields.description: Write zero at the video cycle and initial act cycle. At subsequent act cycles, use the incoming count to identify the next uncompleted endpoint in demonstration. Compare the current TCP and the observed motion with that endpoint. Increment by one only if the motion shown has reached it within 1 cm; otherwise preserve the count. Count bypass endpoints and repeated visits separately. An explicitly zero-step action, an incomplete approach or a wait does not advance the count. Record only arrivals already observed, never the endpoint of the action being selected now. e.g. 2
fields.annotation: The number of demonstrated waypoint-to-waypoint legs already completed by the execution at the current observation, excluding the action selected at this cycle. Set to zero at the video cycle and the initial act cycle. Increment when the observed execution reaches the next demonstrated leg endpoint within 1 cm. Count intermediate bypass points as endpoints, not just marked gaps. Repeated visits count separately in chronological order. Do not increment for a motion that executes no steps, an incomplete approach, or a wait. Preserve the count otherwise. e.g. 2

texts.action:
At the video cycle, produce memory only. At execution start, the stick is already at the demonstrated starting point: do not add a grasp, lift or approach action. Use demonstration to reconstruct the ordered planar route of the lower free end of the attached stick. Follow the actual stick tip, not the robot housing or the red marker: a red marker can remain at the previous gap while the tip travels around an obstacle. The white trail helps identify which side was traversed, but is not itself the complete task history.

Identify the ordered legs and assign demonstration frames to their incoming and outgoing segments, including bypasses beside obstacle ends and arrivals at gaps. Approximate 25-control-step boundaries are segmentation aids only: a nearby displayed frame need not show an endpoint, and elapsed time must not be converted into distance by assuming constant speed. Reconstruct unsampled endpoints geometrically as described below. Use the full video to distinguish retracing a bypass from continuing around the opposite end. Preserve all repetitions as separate chronological occurrences; reaching a previously visited gap does not mean the route is finished. Do not force bypass turns on opposite-direction traversals to share coordinates merely because they pass the same obstacle end. Do not assume that all obstacles must be visited or that every traversal alternates sides.

Identify the stick as the narrow rigid extension beneath the hand and track the centre of its distal end through the demonstration. At the initial act cycle, project the reported TCP into the current execution view to check which visible feature represents the free tip at z=0.07 m; do not transfer a constant image-space offset to other poses. For each usable demonstration frame, measure that same distal-tip feature, not the lowest pixel of the hand, the shaft centre, robot housing, marker or trail. An occluded distal end is an unavailable tip measurement, not permission to substitute a nearby feature. Convert its pixel (u,v) into world coordinates using the camera calibration: C=-R^T t, d=R^T K^-1[u,v,1]^T, and X=C+((0.07-C_z)/d_z)d. Perform this ray-plane calculation rather than estimating metric offsets visually.

Before fitting an unsampled turn, assign each measurement to its chronological leg. Use the preceding arrival and samples strictly before the turn for the incoming segment, and samples strictly after the turn and the following arrival for the outgoing segment. Do not treat a departure sample as evidence of the preceding arrival. Fit the incoming and outgoing planar directions using multiple frames wherever available, preferentially using clear interior distal-tip measurements; downweight uncertain measurements and exclude occluded-tip substitutions. Fit both world x and y freely: an apparently axial image trajectory or vertical shaft does not justify preserving a current world coordinate. Extend both fitted segments to their intersection to recover the shared endpoint; with noisy observations, use a joint least-squares fit with a shared endpoint. Do not interpolate directly between the last incoming sample and first outgoing sample, which cuts across the corner. Those two samples alone do not determine two directions: use neighboring frames farther along each segment, clearly observed start or arrival positions, and obstacle geometry as additional constraints. For collinear reversals, where line intersection does not determine the endpoint, use observed arrival or repeated-visit evidence and gap geometry rather than inventing an intersection. Project the recovered endpoint and both fitted segments back into the demonstration. Check that the assigned distal-tip observations lie on their respective segments in chronological order, that the endpoint follows the last incoming observation and precedes the first outgoing observation along the route, and that the demonstrated obstacle side is preserved. Reject an endpoint supported by extending only one fitted direction, misassigned arrival/departure evidence, or a rounded trail corner treated as a straight tip trajectory. If directions remain underconstrained, use adjoining arrival evidence and other demonstrated views of the same geometric location; do not invent a longer clearance move. When the tip is occluded, use neighboring visible tip positions, shaft and trail evidence, and obstacle geometry as supporting constraints; do not substitute shaft or trail pixels into the tip-height projection.

For a gap arrival, distinguish the full arrival from a sample still approaching the gap. Locate the endpoint from incoming and outgoing path evidence, refining it with the marked gap center only when the marker's own plane is established. Recover the marker's planar coordinates on that plane, then set the commanded TCP height to 0.07 m; never project a ground-marker pixel onto the tip-height plane. Gather arrival and departure evidence from all demonstrated visits to the same static gap to constrain its common location, including the retained starting view and any clear final visit. A still-approaching sample constrains the incoming segment, not the arrival position. Share the gap location without merging chronological occurrences: each visit consumes its own leg. Do not impose shared coordinates on bypass turns merely because they pass the same obstacle end. For the final endpoint, explicitly identify the distal-tip centre in the final demonstration frame and corroborate the feature identification with preceding arrival frames. Apply the calibrated z=0.07 m ray-plane calculation to that pixel and reproject the resulting coordinate to check numerical consistency; reprojection alone does not establish that the chosen feature is the tip. Discard any pixel/world-coordinate pair that disagrees under the calibration and resolve the measurement rather than accepting either as authoritative. If the final tip is occluded, use the existing occlusion and arrival-evidence rules, not a shaft or trail substitute. Do not extrapolate beyond the supported stopping point to a nominal gap coordinate or nominal leg length.

Use current front and wrist observations to refine alignment with the same static obstacle arrangement. Colors identify obstacles within the episode but do not define a universal route.

First evaluate whether the current observation completes the next leg, according to the completed_legs memory rule. With the resulting completed count c, command the endpoint of leg c+1. Set TCP z to 0.07 m and preserve the current approximately downward orientation, normalizing equivalent roll angles if needed. Keep the gripper closed; its command is ignored for this stick tool. Command the reconstructed absolute full leg endpoint, without coarse centimetre-scale rounding or added obstacle clearance. Neither a nominal leg length nor a fixed axial or diagonal offset defines that endpoint. Do not insert arbitrary small subdivisions, lift over an obstacle, or move directly across an obstacle to a later gap. Accept normal arrival error within 1 cm and move on instead of issuing a redundant correction to a reached endpoint.

If the expected endpoint has not been reached, retain the count and complete that leg. If localization is ambiguous, use the retained video's neighboring frames and the current wrist view to select the endpoint consistent with both route order and obstacle clearance; never choose a later occurrence merely because it is closer. If a direct recovery would intersect an obstacle, make a conservative planar correction toward the demonstrated safe corridor without advancing the count until its endpoint is reached. Do not issue an identical-pose motion. If all demonstrated legs are complete and the environment has not yet terminated, hold with a short wait solely to allow terminal evaluation; do not start an extra loop.
